chapter_theme: The first run of Pattinathar's பொது (unplaced) verses, addressed mostly to his own heart: an inventory of the beggar's riches, a loincloth, a porch, leaves, water and the Lord's name, against the wealth, wives, children and kin that go only as far as the mouth, the street and the burning ground. The eyeless needle that will not come on the last road is the chapter's emblem. The Lord is not in stone and copper but in the word, the sky and the devotees; the body is the enjoyment of deeds and goes when they end; the detached cannot be told from worldly people; and the run ends with Siva come as a street beggar to seek the poet, and with a bliss beyond yoga's eight limbs that has swallowed him.
structure_note: The verses fall into loose groups: the beggar's inventory and the heart's folly (329 to 333), where the Lord dwells and what the body is (334, 335), the eyeless needle (336 to 339), what goes how far (340, 341), the body and the beggar's contentment (342 to 347), two verses of உபதேசம் to the heart (348, 349), and a close in the first person on the Lord's doing, the beggar-guru and the bliss beyond yoga (350 to 353). Verses 338 and 339 share the refrain காதற்ற ஊசியும் வாராது காணும் கடைவழிக்கே.

329.reading: There is a loincloth to wear, an outer porch to sleep on, fallen leaves to eat here, water to drink, and for company the holy name of the Lord who rides the bull; in this world, what if the northern horn stands high or the southern horn leans, for the crescent in the sky?
329.nuance: The last line is proverbial: which horn of the moon is higher changes nothing for the moon, so the world's ups and downs change nothing for one who has these five things. அடைகாய் இலை may be the leaf used to wrap betel, or fallen leaves; either way the food is what no one owns.

330.reading: Release is ours: Thiruvalangadu. The bowl the Pure One gave us is a vessel that never runs dry; we have a thriving, wealthy land that gives whatever we ask, good heart. Is there anyone here to be called our equal?
330.nuance: வீடு is both house and release, so the first line gives the beggar a home and salvation in one word, and the shrine where tradition places his end. The wealth claimed is the begging bowl and the land that fills it; ஈடு, an equal, mocks the rich by their own measure.

331.reading: You did not set your sight on the Lord and seek him; you did not seek, dance and grow clear about the Master's feet; saying 'the world's maya has come and covered us' and 'Kama's weapons have raged', will you let yourself be gripped, heart? There are no madmen like you.
331.nuance: The heart's excuses, maya and Kama, are quoted back to it as the things it chose to be caught by, so the verse denies that they are forces one merely suffers. பித்தர், madman, is Siva's own epithet elsewhere; here it is only abuse.

332.reading: One hand doing the rite, one eye wandering, one mind calculating, one false and deceitful tongue speaking, one flesh-smelling body leaning on something, one ear wanting to hear something else: how will you accept the puja I perform, remover of deeds?
332.nuance: ஒன்று repeats for each organ to show them each doing a different thing: the puja is performed by a body whose parts are not together. The poet does not say puja is worthless, only that his is divided, and leaves the acceptance to the Lord.

333.reading: There are eyes to see and a mind to look, a melting heart and a tune to sing, ears to hear, and fresh leaves to count out and offer; and while the Lord stands before you, you go to the earth. Alas, ruin on you, you humans!
333.nuance: The verse answers 332 from the other side: there the organs were present and divided, here they are present and unused. மண்ணுண்டு போகுது, going to eat earth, is dying unused; ஈசன் இருக்கையிலே, with the Lord right there, is the shrine or the inner presence, the verse does not say which.

334.reading: In the word and at the end of the word, in the Vedic hearing, in the night and in the stainless sky, in the house of those who have inquired and finished, and among the devotees: these are the places where the Lord stays. Will our brow-eyed one dwell in stone and in copper?
334.nuance: The question is rhetorical and the answer the verse expects is no, but the list before it is not a denial of place: the Lord is in speech, scripture, sky, the jnani's house and the devotees, so the attack is on the material image, not on worship. அல்லில், in the night, may be darkness as the unmanifest or a corrupt word.

335.reading: See, a body is only the enjoyment of deeds; see, once the deeds are spent it will not stay the time of a millet grain. It joins those who think of Siva's feet and leaves those who do not. If you stand on this path, mind, is there anyone like you, my own kin?
335.nuance: The third line is ambiguous: the subject of மேவும் and நீங்கி may be Siva's foot, which comes to those who remember it, or the body-and-deeds of the first two lines. The first reading fits the exhortation that follows; both make remembrance the hinge. The mind is called உற்றவர், one's own, in contrast to 312 where every kin is an enemy.

336.reading: Tearing the silk, taking out the thick needle with care, rolling it up tight and giving it into the hands of my wife with her swarming hair; was it so that all the desire of this heavy maya-woman, who held me bound, should leave and part from me that Siva turned back like this?
336.nuance: The verse belongs to the story of Pattinathar's renunciation, in which a needle sent to him in a box carried the message that not even an eyeless needle goes with one at death; the details of silk and rolling cannot be recovered from the verse alone. கனமாயக்காரி, the heavy sorceress, is the wife as maya; சிவன் மீண்டது, Siva turning back or returning, is the poet's name for what happened to him.

337.reading: Deceitful breasts, union with deer-like women, the wealth that surrounds: what could they do for the fight that has come upon me? Was it so that, by merit I had done, I might clear myself from the mind of the faultless king, that he put the eyeless needle into my hand?
337.nuance: போதுற்ற பூசல், the battle that has arrived, is death or the crisis of renunciation. தீதற்ற மன்னவன் சிந்தையினின்று தெளிவதற்கோ is obscure: to grow clear within the mind of the faultless Lord, or to escape the king's notice, as in the legend of the poet's trial. The one who gave the needle is read as the Lord acting through the sender.

338.reading: Heart that always takes refuge in the flower feet of Annamalai of the strong shoulders that stood in contest: in this world the riches you sought as wealth and the treasure you buried, see, not even an eyeless needle will come on the final road.
338.nuance: The eyeless needle is the least thing that could be carried and the one the legend made the poet's emblem; the refrain line is shared with 339. The buried treasure is the hoarder's form of wealth, kept for a journey on which it cannot be taken.

339.reading: Did you not hear the word of the one who taught the inner meaning of the Veda, to give up the woman and the hunger for land? When, through merit done, it grows bright like the sun and the moon, see, not even an eyeless needle comes on the final road.
339.nuance: Who the teacher of the Veda's inner meaning is, the guru or the Lord, is not said. The third line is loose: the subject of வெளிச்சமதாம் (becomes light) may be the inner meaning made clear by merit, or the poet himself at the moment of death. The refrain fixes the sense: nothing goes with one.

340.reading: Wife, children, livelihood and wealth reach only as far as one's own mouth; the kin of one's own kind only as far as the cremation ground. What is the companion for the road? Even a millet grain or a sesame seed of austerity done before is what rules; the other world is truly attained.
340.nuance: The verse measures each possession by how far it goes: wealth to the mouth, kin to the burning ground, tapas beyond. தனை ஆள, 'to rule', is read as the tapas that governs what follows; the syntax is compressed and it could also be 'to make it one's own'. பரலோகம் சித்திக்கும் is the plain promise of a next world that the Siddhars elsewhere mock.

341.reading: Property and livelihood go only as far as the house; the women with arrow-eyes streaming tears only as far as the street; the children who sob with both hands on their heads only as far as the burning ground. What follows, clinging, is the pair of deeds, merit and sin.
341.nuance: A variation on 340 with the stations made concrete: house, street, cremation ground. பற்றித் தொடரும், what follows holding on, inverts the word for attachment: what one clung to stays behind, what clings to one is karma.

342.reading: Pus, blood, rich fluid and slime pressed together and rising and flowing, when there is not even a cloth to cover it, day and night; the womb that flies and ants enter: for the humans who die day and night there is no medicine to keep them from dying.
342.nuance: The syntax is broken across the lines and the verse may be corrupt: the yoni in line 3 is where flies and ants enter, which can be the womb one is born from or the dead body's orifices. The close is a direct denial of the medical Siddhars' claim: there is no remedy against death.

343.reading: For the cold frost there is a tight rag; when hunger comes each day there is rice in every house for you to eat; when the thought rises there are good women for hire in the streets of this world. Why, heart, have you grown weary, always wounding yourself?
343.nuance: The third line is the surprise: the beggar's inventory of 329 and 344 here includes women for hire. It can be read straight, as a Siddhar's refusal of the ascetic's sexual anxiety, or as the heart's own argument quoted against it, since the heart is reproached for wounding itself. The verse does not resolve it, and I leave both.

344.reading: There are rivers and groves, fine streets and the hall itself; there is water, a rag and a long loincloth, day after day; heart that wanders bewildered, there is going from house to house eating rice, sleeping, and then simply being still; there is joy in that too.
344.nuance: சும்மா இருக்க, to be simply still, is the Siddhars' and later Tamil mystics' name for the state without effort; here it comes after eating and sleeping as the last item on a list of ordinary things, so the highest state is made the plainest.

345.reading: To wear and to cover, when cold wind and sun press close, there is an old dhoti to keep them off; to lie down there are outer porches everywhere in the whole world; when hunger comes there is Siva to give. Heart, we have no lack.
345.nuance: The inventory is the same as 329 and 344, but the giver is named: Siva gives when hunger comes, so the begging bowl is held out to the Lord, not to householders. குறைவில்லை, no lack, is the beggar's word of plenty.

346.reading: 'There are cattle, calves and children': all such rejoicing, we have heard, ends in ruin; now listen, heart. We have a bowl and a rag, the five letters to recite within, and the devotees of the Lord with the earring as our companions too.
346.nuance: தோடுண்ட கண்டன் is read as the Lord who wears the earring, after தோடுடைய செவியன்; கண்டன் may also be 'the one of the throat' (that held the poison). The inventory adds two things the earlier ones lacked: the mantra inside and the devotees outside.

347.reading: Do those who have left the great states and the bewilderment of the city of maya have any fixed observance? Loving the Eternal, when they sweat they bathe, when hungry they eat, they close their eyes and sleep; looked at, those free of attachment are just like the people of the world.
347.nuance: மாத்தான அவத்தை is unclear: the great states (the avasthas of the soul, as in 353) or great hardship. நிஷ்டை is fixed practice or a vow; the verse says the detached have none, and that from outside they are indistinguishable from the worldly, which turns the usual complaint about sham ascetics inside out.

348.reading: Hold that there is one; hold that God exists; hold that all high wealth is nothing; look at the face of the hungry; hold that good virtue and friendship are good; without leaving the middle, be always as it has been set for us. Heart, this is the teaching for you.
348.nuance: The teaching is in the imperative இரு, 'be', repeated for each clause, so it is a way of standing rather than a doctrine. ஒன்றென்றிரு may be 'be one' or 'hold that it is one'; நமக்கிட்டபடி, as set for us, accepts what is apportioned, the Kural's ஊழ், without naming it.

349.reading: Hold the feet of the true guru as your aim and trust them; hold the wretched body as a puppet show; hold the crowd of kin as a heap of rags pressed together, and life as water from an overturned pot. Heart, this is the teaching for you.
349.nuance: The second உபதேசம் verse gives one positive item, the guru's feet, and three figures for what to let go: the body as a doll dance, kin as bundled rags, life as water running out. குடங்கவிழ் நீர் is the pot tipped over: once it has started to pour, nothing holds it.

350.reading: Nothing whatever is my doing; now, God, I have come to know that all is your doing. Since I took up this flesh I have done no evil deed; is it then the evil done before this birth that has come and blazed up like this?
350.nuance: The two halves sit uneasily: all is the Lord's doing, yet what has come upon him is explained by his own deeds in a former birth. The verse does not reconcile them; it holds the Saiva position that karma is the Lord's instrument without saying so.

351.reading: Taking a holy guise and walking the street, he came seeking me and said with kindness, 'give alms'; I bowed at the feet of that one. Was it to take me, who was minded to reach the shore of the sea that is the womb, and make me into a form of his own, that Siva came like this?
351.nuance: The beggar at the door who turns out to be Siva is the poet's initiation as tradition tells it. கருவாகும் ஏதக் கடற்கரை is obscure: the shore of the sea of birth, which the poet wished to reach, or a fault (ஏதம்) of the womb. உருவாக்கிக் கொள்ள, to make into his own form, is the guru making the disciple like himself.

352.reading: I have left the world; I do not desire; I will not go near the vain with their two deeds, nor listen to their words, which are ruin; I have touched the state in which truth does not decay; I have cast off joy and sorrow; and the Supreme that the ancient four Vedas say they do not reach has come to me here.
352.nuance: The verse is a series of first-person perfects, the poet's own account of arrival, unusual in a chapter of questions and exhortations. நான்மறைக்கும் எட்டேன் எனும் பரம், the Supreme that says even to the four Vedas 'I am not reached', comes of itself (வந்து எய்தியது), so the reaching is the Lord's.

353.reading: Having left and climbed past the eight-limbed yoga, the six supports and the five states, in the open space I saw one wonder: growing round and drinking the milk that wells from the red moon, rejoicing, a great bliss that cannot be cut has swallowed me.
353.nuance: The verse lists the yogic system (ashtanga, the six adharas, the five avasthas) only to pass beyond it; the open space (வெளி) is the same term as 304. செம்மதிப் பாலூறல், the milk welling from the red moon, is the Siddhars' cipher for the nectar held to drip from the moon-centre at the head, as tradition reads it; வட்டாகி, becoming round, may be the moon's fullness or the poet's. The bliss swallows the poet, not the poet the bliss.

links.note: The Kural curses the creator if even begging is needed to live: let the one who made the world wander and perish. Pattinathar lists loincloth, porch, leaves, water and the Lord's name as enough, and 345 adds that when hunger comes Siva gives. On the Kural's plain reading a life sustained by begging is an indictment of the world's order; on Pattinathar's, it is the life in which nothing is lacking. The conflict holds if both speak of the same begging; the Kural's chapter is about want forced on a man, Pattinathar's about want chosen.

Tirumular lists curd, ghee, copper, mercury, brick, bilva and gold as materials any one of which can be the Sivalinga; Pattinathar asks whether the brow-eyed one will dwell in stone and copper and expects the answer no. On the reading that Pattinathar denies the Lord's presence in the material image, the two conflict directly; the conflict softens only if his line means that the Lord is not confined to stone, which the preceding list of the Lord's dwellings does not say.

Sivavakkiyar names brick, black stone, the red lingam, copper and brass as the things people say Siva dwells in and sends them to know themselves instead; Pattinathar asks whether the Lord will dwell in stone and copper and places him in the word, the sky, the jnani's house and the devotees. Both make the same denial; Pattinathar supplies the positive list that Sivavakkiyar's verse leaves to the dance in the hall.

Both set kin below deeds: Tirumular says the kin who cling and follow are worse than one's karma and tells one to light the lamp of awareness before the life leaves; Pattinathar says kin go only as far as the cremation ground and that only tapas done before goes further. Each names what one should secure while alive, awareness or austerity.

The Kural says to do virtue without delay, since at death it is the companion that does not perish; Pattinathar measures property to the house, wives to the street and children to the burning ground, and says what follows is the pair of deeds, merit and sin. The Kural names only the good companion; Pattinathar adds that sin follows just as faithfully.

Sivavakkiyar asks whether goats, lands, elephants, armies or a crore of horses will come and stand beside you, and answers that only the alms thrown and the dharma done gladly do; Pattinathar's wealth, wives and children stop at the house, street and burning ground, and only merit and sin follow. Both use the image of what accompanies one, and both make deeds the only companion.

Tirumular's drinkers of Siva's bliss keep it standing, sitting and lying down; Pattinathar's detached ones bathe, eat and sleep like everyone else and have no fixed observance. Both place the attained state inside ordinary postures and acts rather than in a visible discipline.

The Kural says that removing the ruinous hunger of the destitute is where wealth should be stored; Pattinathar's teaching to his heart is to hold wealth as nothing and look at the face of the hungry (பசித்தோர் முகம் பார்). The Kural keeps wealth and redirects it; Pattinathar has already dismissed it and keeps only the looking.

Both have Siva as the beggar: Tirumular's righteous one, with no one of his own, dwells in the burning ground, eats alms and is the model renouncer; Pattinathar's Siva takes a holy guise, walks the street and asks him for alms, and that asking is the poet's initiation. In Tirumular the Lord's begging is an example; in Pattinathar it is the means by which he takes a disciple.

Both describe release as leaving the yogic and psychological apparatus behind: Tirumular puts away the five states and the false thirty-six tattvas and stands as one; Pattinathar climbs past the eight-limbed yoga, the six supports and the five states into the open space. Tirumular ends in standing as one, Pattinathar in being swallowed by bliss.

Both have the nectar that wells for the one who has gone within: Tirumular's seeker goes within the bright flame in the full lotus and the nectar flows; Pattinathar drinks the milk that wells from the red moon in the open space beyond the six supports. Both place the drink above the centres, and both make it the mark of arrival rather than a stage.

source_issues: The பொது run (own ids 0270-5.1 onward) is printed without word spacing in the source, so word division is the marker's; 342 in particular has broken syntax across lines and may be corrupt.
343 includes women for hire among the beggar's provisions; the line reads as printed and is not emended, but it sits oddly with the rest of the inventory verses.
